learning_activity_name: Describe the concept of food and nutrition (meaning and importance)
sla_name: Meaning and importance of food and nutrition
sla_assessment_criteria: The concept of food and nutrition is well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Food items|Pictures/charts/ video/diagrams showing different types of food items
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Food is any substance eaten to supply the body with nutrients, while nutrition is the process by which the body takes in, digests, absorbs and uses food. Students learn why both are vital for life.
sla_notes_details: Food is any solid or liquid that, when eaten, provides energy, builds and repairs body tissues, and regulates body processes. A nutrient is a chemical substance in food that the body needs: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and dietary fibre. Nutrition includes ingestion, digestion, absorption, transport, utilisation and excretion. Importance: it gives energy for work and play, supports growth in children, repairs worn tissues, protects the body from disease, regulates body temperature and helps mental development. Other terms are diet (the food normally eaten), health (physical, mental and social well-being) and malnutrition (poor nutrition due to deficiency or excess).
sla_notes_illustrations: A student who skips breakfast feels weak and inattentive by mid-morning, whereas a student who eats ugali with beans and fruit has energy for lessons. The class lists foods eaten at home and states the main role of each.
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowing the value of food helps families choose meals that keep children healthy, active and able to learn.
sla_exercise: Define nutrition.::The process by which the body takes in, digests, absorbs and uses food.||State three importance of food.::Gives energy, builds and repairs the body, protects against disease (regulates body processes).||What is a nutrient?::A chemical substance in food that the body needs, such as protein or vitamin C.

sla_notes_intro: Food and Human Nutrition draws on and supports other school subjects. Students explore these links using ICT and other sources.
sla_notes_details: Biology explains digestion, cells and the functions of nutrients; Chemistry explains carbohydrates, proteins, fats and food preservation; Physics explains heat transfer (conduction, convection, radiation) in cooking; Mathematics is used for measuring ingredients, proportions, costing and budgeting; Geography relates to food production, climate and crops; Agriculture supplies raw food materials; Commerce and Book-keeping help with menu costing and food business; Civics and Life skills relate to health and hygiene; Textile and Garment Construction relates to kitchen clothing and aprons. Language subjects help in writing recipes and reports.
sla_notes_illustrations: In preparing 2 kg of maize flour ugali for 10 students, Mathematics is used to compute 200 g per person, Physics explains why a lid speeds up boiling, and Biology explains the energy obtained from carbohydrate.
sla_notes_daily_life: Seeing the links helps a student apply knowledge from many subjects in the kitchen, in a food business or in managing a household.
sla_exercise: Which subject explains digestion of food?::Biology.||Name the subject used for measuring ingredients and costing.::Mathematics.||How does Physics relate to cooking?::It explains heat transfer such as conduction, convection and radiation.

sla_name: Food groups

sla_teaching_aids: Food items|Chart/pictures depicting different food groups
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Foods are classified into groups according to the nutrients they mainly supply. Students learn the five groups and examples in Tanzania.
sla_notes_details: The groups are: (1) cereals, roots, tubers and green bananas, e.g. maize, rice, millet, sorghum, cassava, sweet potatoes, plantains, which give carbohydrates and energy; (2) foods of animal origin, legumes and pulses, e.g. meat, fish, eggs, milk, beans, peas, groundnuts, which give protein, iron and B vitamins; (3) vegetables, e.g. spinach, amaranth, cabbage, carrots, which give vitamins, minerals and fibre; (4) fruits, e.g. mango, orange, pawpaw, banana, which give vitamin C and other vitamins; (5) sugar, honey, oils and fats, e.g. cooking oil, butter, groundnut oil, which give concentrated energy. Water is needed in addition. A balanced diet includes foods from all groups.
sla_notes_illustrations: Meal of ugali (group 1), beans (group 2), spinach (group 3) and an orange (group 4) with a little cooking oil (group 5) covers all groups in one day's lunch.
sla_notes_daily_life: Choosing from each food group at every meal guards against hunger and deficiency diseases, even on a small budget.
sla_exercise: Name a food from the fruit group.::Mango, orange, pawpaw or banana.||Which group supplies most of the energy?::Cereals, roots, tubers and green bananas (also fats and oils and sugar).||Give two legumes.::Beans and peas (also groundnuts, lentils).

sla_name: Nutrient content of foods: types, functions and stability
sla_assessment_criteria: Nutrient contents in different foods are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Chart depicting types|Sources|Functions of different nutrients
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Nutrients are the useful components of food. Students study each type, its function, sources and how it is affected during cooking.
sla_notes_details: Carbohydrates (starch, sugars, fibre) give energy, 4 kcal per gram; sources are cereals, tubers and sugar. Proteins (made of amino acids) build and repair tissues; sources are meat, fish, eggs, beans; deficiency causes kwashiorkor. Fats and oils give concentrated energy (9 kcal per gram), carry vitamins A, D, E and K and protect organs. Vitamins: A (vision, skin), B group (nerves, energy release), C (healing, resistance), D (bones), K (blood clotting). Minerals: calcium (bones, teeth), iron (haemoglobin), iodine (thyroid), zinc, fluoride. Water regulates temperature and transports nutrients. Stability: vitamin C and folate are destroyed by heat, air and long cooking and dissolve in water; fat-soluble vitamins are fairly stable; proteins coagulate on heating; starch gelatinises; minerals are stable but leach into cooking water.
sla_notes_illustrations: Boiling spinach for a long time in a large volume of water and discarding the water loses vitamin C and minerals, while steaming or cooking quickly with little water retains them.
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowing how nutrients are lost helps you cook to keep the nutritional value of family meals.
sla_exercise: Which nutrient builds and repairs body tissues?::Protein.||Give one function of iron.::It forms haemoglobin in red blood cells, carrying oxygen.||Why should vegetables not be overcooked?::Heat and water destroy or remove vitamins such as vitamin C.

sla_name: Balanced meal: meaning, importance and planning factors
sla_method: ICT based learning and Case study
sla_assessment_criteria: The concept of a balanced meal is well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Food items|Chart/pictures depicting different food items
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A balanced meal supplies the required nutrients in correct proportions. Students learn to plan such meals.
sla_notes_details: A balanced meal contains foods from all food groups in suitable amounts to meet the body's needs for energy, growth and protection. Importance: it promotes good health, prevents malnutrition, supports growth, gives good body weight and improves productivity. Factors to consider when planning: age, sex, occupation and activity level, state of health, physiological state (pregnancy, lactation), nutrient needs, cost and budget, availability and season of foods, cultural and religious beliefs, food preferences and likes, number of people, time and skills available, variety, colour, texture and flavour, and facilities and equipment.
sla_notes_illustrations: Plan lunch for a family of five with a limited budget: rice (energy), beans with tomato sauce (protein), sautéed cabbage (vitamins) and a banana (fruit). The meal is cheap, seasonal and balanced.
sla_notes_daily_life: Planning balanced meals within your budget keeps the family healthy and avoids wastage of food and money.
sla_exercise: Define a balanced meal.::A meal containing foods from all food groups in the correct proportions to meet the body's needs.||Name three factors considered when planning meals.::Age, cost, availability, health status, cultural beliefs (any three).||Why is variety in colour and texture important?::It makes the meal attractive and appetising.

sla_name: Food, kitchen and personal hygiene
sla_assessment_criteria: Food, kitchen and personal hygiene in food preparation, cooking and serving are clearly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures depicting food|Kitchen|Personal hygiene practices
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Hygiene in preparing, cooking and serving food prevents food poisoning and disease. Students explore the three kinds of hygiene.
sla_notes_details: Personal hygiene: bathe daily, wash hands with soap before handling food and after using the toilet, keep nails short and clean, wear clean apron and head cover, tie back long hair, cover cuts with waterproof dressing, and do not cough or sneeze over food. Food hygiene: buy fresh food, wash fruits and vegetables, store raw and cooked foods separately, cook thoroughly, keep food covered, refrigerate perishables and use safe water. Kitchen hygiene: clean surfaces, utensils and cookers after use, wash dishes with hot soapy water and rinse, dry and store properly, dispose of waste in covered bins, control flies, rodents and cockroaches, and keep the sink drained.
sla_notes_illustrations: A cook who wipes the chopping board used for raw fish and then cuts tomatoes on it spreads bacteria; the correct way is to wash and sanitise the board or use a separate one for cooked and ready-to-eat foods.
sla_notes_daily_life: Good hygiene at home and in food business protects families and customers from typhoid, cholera and diarrhoea.
sla_exercise: Why should you wash hands before handling food?::To remove germs that could contaminate the food.||State two rules of kitchen hygiene.::Clean surfaces and utensils after use, and dispose of waste in covered bins.||Why keep raw and cooked food separate?::To prevent cross-contamination.

sla_name: Safety in the kitchen
sla_assessment_criteria: Safety in the kitchen is well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures showing common accidents in the kitchen|Charts showing safety precautions
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Kitchens contain heat, sharp tools and electricity, so accidents can occur. Students learn precautions and first aid for common accidents.
sla_notes_details: Common accidents: burns and scalds (from hot liquids, steam, oil), cuts (from knives), falls (wet floors), electric shocks, fire, and poisoning from chemicals or spoiled food. Precautions: turn pot handles inward, use dry oven gloves, keep a safe distance from hot oil, never leave cooking unattended, keep knives sharp and use a chopping board, carry knives pointing down, wipe spills immediately, keep flammable items away from flames, check gas and electrical connections, use dry hands with electricity, store chemicals in labelled containers and keep a first-aid kit and fire extinguisher or sand available. First aid for burns: cool with running water for 10 minutes and cover clean.
sla_notes_illustrations: A cook who leaves a pot handle sticking out risks knocking it and getting scalded; turning the handle inward removes the danger.
sla_notes_daily_life: Following safety rules at home and at work prevents injuries that cause pain, cost and loss of time.
sla_exercise: Name two common kitchen accidents.::Burns and cuts.||First aid for a minor burn?::Cool it with running water for about ten minutes and cover with a clean dressing.||Why turn pot handles inward?::So they are not knocked over, avoiding scalds.

sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Fruits and vegetables are protective foods rich in vitamins, minerals and fibre. Students identify types, nutritive value and selection.
sla_notes_details: Vegetable types: leafy (spinach, kale, amaranth), roots (carrot, beetroot), fruit vegetables (tomato, eggplant, pepper, cucumber), flowers (cauliflower, broccoli), stems (celery), bulbs (onion, garlic), seeds and pods (peas, green beans). Fruit types: citrus (orange, lemon), tropical (mango, pineapple, pawpaw), berries, stone fruits (mango, plum), and pomes (apple). Nutritive value: vitamins A and C, iron, calcium, fibre and water; fruits also contain natural sugars. Selection: fresh, firm, bright colour, free from bruises and pests. Storage: cool, dry, ventilated place; leafy vegetables wrapped in damp cloth. Cooking should be brief to retain nutrients.
sla_notes_illustrations: Students classify a basket containing carrot, spinach, tomato, onion and orange and state the main vitamin supplied by each: carrot (vitamin A), spinach (iron), orange (vitamin C).
sla_notes_daily_life: Eating a variety of fruits and vegetables daily protects against illness and can be grown cheaply in a home garden.
sla_exercise: Give one leafy vegetable.::Spinach, kale or amaranth.||Which vitamin do oranges provide?::Vitamin C.||State one sign of a fresh vegetable.::Bright colour and firm texture.

sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Beverages are drinks and appetizers are small foods served to stimulate appetite. Students learn their meaning and types.
sla_notes_details: Beverages: alcoholic and non-alcoholic; non-alcoholic ones are hot (tea, coffee, cocoa, milk drinks) and cold (fruit juices, squashes, milkshakes, soda, water, smoothies, traditional drinks). Appetizers (starters) are served before the main meal: hors d'oeuvres, canapés, cocktails, soups, salads, fruit cocktails and dips. Purposes: to stimulate appetite, to introduce a meal and to give variety. Qualities: small portion, attractive colour, light flavour, served cold or hot as suitable, and balanced with the main course.
sla_notes_illustrations: A wedding menu may begin with a fruit cocktail and small samosa canapés, followed by a main course of pilau, and finish with a chilled passion fruit juice.
sla_notes_daily_life: Beverages and appetizers are important in receptions, small food businesses and family celebrations.
sla_exercise: What is an appetizer?::A small food served before the main meal to stimulate the appetite.||Give two hot beverages.::Tea and coffee (cocoa).||Name two cold beverages.::Fruit juice and milkshake (squash).

sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Pulses, nuts and oil seeds are important plant sources of protein. Students study types, nutritive value and uses.
sla_notes_details: Pulses are dried edible seeds of legumes: beans, peas, lentils, cowpeas, pigeon peas, green grams and chickpeas. Nuts include groundnuts, cashew nuts, coconut, almonds; oil seeds include sunflower, sesame, cotton seed and soya bean. Nutritive value: protein, carbohydrates, B vitamins, iron and fibre; nuts and oil seeds also contain fat (oil). Uses: stews and sauces, flour for porridge, fillings, snacks, milk (soya), oil extraction and cakes. Soaking before cooking shortens time, and the proteins are incomplete but improved by combining with cereals.
sla_notes_illustrations: A meal of maize and beans (githeri) gives a mixture of cereal and pulse proteins that together supply all essential amino acids.
sla_notes_daily_life: Pulses and nuts are cheap protein sources for families who cannot always afford meat or fish.
sla_exercise: Give two examples of pulses.::Beans and lentils (peas, green grams).||Which nutrient do pulses mainly supply?::Protein.||Why soak pulses before cooking?::To soften them and reduce cooking time.

sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Proper nutrition is the basis of good health. Students discuss how good and poor nutrition affect the body.
sla_notes_details: Good nutrition supports growth and development, strong immunity, healthy skin, hair, teeth and bones, good vision, mental alertness, reproductive health and energy for activities, and reduces the risk of diseases such as obesity, diabetes, heart disease and anaemia. Poor nutrition leads to underweight, stunting, wasting, deficiency diseases (night blindness, rickets, goitre, scurvy) and reduced productivity. Guidelines: eat a variety of foods, limit sugar, salt and saturated fat, drink enough water, control portion size and eat regular meals.
sla_notes_illustrations: A child who drinks milk and eats vegetables and fish grows tall and strong, while one on a starchy diet only may show signs of stunting or anaemia.
sla_notes_daily_life: Good eating habits reduce medical expenses and keep people productive at school and work.
sla_exercise: Name one disease caused by lack of vitamin C.::Scurvy.||State one benefit of proper nutrition.::Strong immunity, growth or energy (any one).||Which mineral prevents goitre?::Iodine.

sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Diet, health and physical activity are linked; energy taken in must match energy used. Students explore this balance.
sla_notes_details: Energy balance: energy intake from food (kcal or kJ) versus energy expenditure through basal metabolism, physical activity and digestion. If intake exceeds expenditure, the extra is stored as fat and can cause overweight and obesity; if intake is lower, the body loses weight. Regular physical activity strengthens muscles and bones, improves circulation, helps control weight and reduces stress. Active people need more energy and protein than those who are sedentary. Guidelines: at least 30 minutes of moderate exercise daily and a diet rich in whole foods, water and less sugar.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student who eats chips and soda daily but never exercises may gain weight, while a footballer with the same diet uses the energy in training.
sla_notes_daily_life: Combining balanced eating with regular exercise helps prevent lifestyle diseases such as diabetes and hypertension.
sla_exercise: What happens if energy intake exceeds energy used?::The excess is stored as fat, leading to overweight.||Give one benefit of regular physical activity.::Stronger muscles and bones (or controlling weight).||Name one lifestyle disease.::Diabetes, hypertension or obesity.

sla_notes_intro: Eating disorders are serious abnormal eating behaviours that harm health. Students learn their types, causes and prevention.
sla_notes_details: Main types: anorexia nervosa (severe restriction of food and fear of weight gain), bulimia nervosa (binge eating followed by vomiting or laxative use) and binge eating disorder (repeated uncontrolled overeating). Causes include body-image pressure, peer influence, media, stress, low self-esteem and family issues. Signs are extreme weight change, skipping meals, obsession with calories, fatigue, dizziness and withdrawal. Effects: malnutrition, weak bones, heart problems, dental damage and depression. Prevention and care: positive body image, balanced diet, support from family and friends, and counselling and medical help.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student who stops eating to look thin and becomes dizzy in class needs support from parents, the teacher and a health worker.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding these disorders helps you support friends and encourages healthy attitudes to food and body image.
sla_exercise: Name two eating disorders.::Anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa.||Give one cause of eating disorders.::Body-image pressure (or stress, low self-esteem).||How can they be treated?::With counselling, medical help and family support.

sla_notes_intro: Beverages and appetizers are prepared using different methods and standards. Students describe these methods.
sla_notes_details: Tea: boil water, add tea leaves or bags, brew 3 to 5 minutes, strain, serve with milk and sugar. Coffee: infuse ground coffee in hot water. Cocoa: mix cocoa powder with sugar and a little cold milk into a paste, add hot milk and simmer. Fruit juice: wash and peel fruit, blend or squeeze, strain, sweeten and chill. Milkshake: blend cold milk with fruit or flavouring. Appetizers: canapés are assembled on a bread or biscuit base with toppings; salads are washed, cut, arranged and dressed at the last moment; soups are made by sautéing, adding stock and simmering. Points: use fresh ingredients, correct measurements, clean equipment, attractive garnish and correct serving temperature.
sla_notes_illustrations: To make passion fruit juice: scoop pulp, blend with water, strain, add sugar to taste, chill and serve garnished with a slice of orange.
sla_notes_daily_life: These skills are useful for home hospitality and for small businesses such as juice sellers and caterers.
sla_exercise: Why is salad dressing added at the last moment?::So that vegetables stay crisp and do not become soggy.||State one step in making fruit juice.::Blend or squeeze the fruit and strain it.||Serve milkshake hot or cold?::Cold.

sla_notes_details: Practical procedure: read the recipe, plan the work order and time, wash hands, put on apron, assemble ingredients and equipment, measure accurately, prepare and cook, garnish, serve and clean up. sla_notes_intro: Pulses and nuts are prepared by soaking, boiling, roasting, frying and grinding. Students describe methods for making dishes.
sla_notes_details: Preparation of pulses: sort and wash, soak for several hours, discard soaking water, boil until soft (add salt near the end), then use in stews, soups and salads or mash for fritters. Do not add bicarbonate of soda because it destroys thiamine. Nuts: shell, roast in a dry pan or oven, fry, grind into paste (peanut butter) or milk, or add to salads and sweets. Dishes: bean stew, lentil soup, chickpea curry, bean fritters (maharage vitumbua) and groundnut sauce. Points: cook thoroughly to remove anti-nutritional factors and season for flavour.
sla_notes_illustrations: For bean stew: soak beans overnight, boil until tender, fry onions and tomatoes, add beans with cooking liquid, simmer and season.
sla_notes_daily_life: These methods make low-cost, nutritious meals for families and school feeding programmes.
sla_exercise: Why soak pulses?::To soften them and reduce cooking time.||Give one method of preparing nuts.::Roasting, grinding or frying.||Name one dish from pulses.::Bean stew, lentil soup or chickpea curry.

sla_name: Food additives
sla_assessment_criteria: Food additives are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Food additives|Pictures/charts showing different food additives
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Food additives are substances added to food to improve its flavour, colour, appearance or keeping quality. Students study herbs, spices, colours, flavourings, preservatives and condiments.
sla_notes_details: Herbs are leaves of aromatic plants (basil, mint, parsley, coriander); spices come from seeds, bark, roots or fruits (cloves, cinnamon, cardamom, pepper, ginger, turmeric, cumin). Food colours may be natural (turmeric, beetroot, saffron) or artificial; flavourings include vanilla, essences and extracts; preservatives (salt, sugar, vinegar, sodium benzoate) slow spoilage; condiments (salt, pepper, mustard, chilli sauce, tomato sauce) are added at the table. Uses: to enhance taste, aroma and appearance, to preserve and to make food more appealing. Precautions: use in correct amounts, choose approved additives, avoid allergens and store spices in airtight containers away from light.
sla_notes_illustrations: Adding cloves, cardamom and cinnamon to rice makes pilau aromatic; a pinch of turmeric gives it a yellow colour.
sla_notes_daily_life: Zanzibar spices are famous, and using them wisely adds flavour and value to everyday meals and to food businesses.
sla_exercise: Give two examples of spices.::Cloves and cinnamon (cardamom, pepper).||What is a preservative?::A substance that slows spoilage and prolongs the keeping quality of food.||Name one natural food colour.::Turmeric (beetroot or saffron).

learning_activity_name: Describe cereals (types, nutritive values, cereal products and uses)
sla_name: Cereals: types, nutritive values, products and uses
sla_assessment_criteria: Cereals are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Cereals|Video/pictures/ charts showing different cereals
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Cereals are grains of cultivated grasses and are the staple foods of many Tanzanians. Students study their structure, nutrition and uses.
sla_notes_details: Main cereals: maize, rice, wheat, sorghum, millet, barley, oats and rye. Structure of a grain: bran (outer layer, fibre and B vitamins), endosperm (starch and some protein) and germ (fat, protein, vitamins). Nutritive value: mainly carbohydrate (about 70 percent), moderate protein (7 to 12 percent), B vitamins and minerals; whole grains contain more fibre. Products: flour, semolina, bread, pasta, breakfast cereals, porridge, popcorn, beer and starch. Uses: staple foods (ugali, rice, chapati), baking, thickening, and animal feed. Milling and polishing remove bran and germ and reduce nutrients. Store in a dry, ventilated, pest-free place.
sla_notes_illustrations: Whole meal flour has more fibre and vitamins than refined white flour; unpolished rice keeps its bran and is more nutritious than polished rice.
sla_notes_daily_life: Cereals are the main energy source for most families, so knowing how to choose and store them improves nutrition and reduces losses.
sla_exercise: Name the three parts of a cereal grain.::Bran, endosperm and germ.||Give two cereal products.::Flour and bread (pasta, porridge).||Why is whole meal flour better than white flour?::It retains bran and germ, so it has more fibre and vitamins.

sla_name: Malnutrition: meaning, types, causes, symptoms and prevention
sla_assessment_criteria: The concept of malnutrition is well explored.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures/charts/ video showing people affected with malnutrition
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Malnutrition is poor nutritional status caused by lack, excess or imbalance of nutrients. Students explore its types and prevention.
sla_notes_details: Types: undernutrition (underweight, wasting, stunting, kwashiorkor from protein deficiency, marasmus from energy and protein deficiency), micronutrient deficiencies (anaemia from iron, goitre from iodine, night blindness from vitamin A, rickets from vitamin D) and overnutrition (overweight and obesity). Causes: poverty, food shortage, poor feeding practices, infections, lack of education, and unbalanced diet. Symptoms: kwashiorkor shows swelling (oedema), thin hair and skin sores; marasmus shows a very thin, wasted body; anaemia shows pallor and tiredness. Prevention: breastfeeding, timely complementary foods, balanced diets, food fortification and supplements, growth monitoring, hygiene and treating infections.
sla_notes_illustrations: A two-year-old with swollen feet, thin reddish hair and irritability, fed mainly on maize porridge, is likely to have kwashiorkor; adding eggs, beans, milk and fish to the diet helps recovery.
sla_notes_daily_life: Recognising malnutrition early helps families and communities take action and protect children.
sla_exercise: Which deficiency causes kwashiorkor?::Protein.||State two symptoms of marasmus.::Severe wasting and very thin body (loose skin).||Give two ways to prevent malnutrition.::Balanced diet and exclusive breastfeeding for six months.

sla_name: Planning balanced meals for different groups
sla_assessment_criteria: Balanced meals for different groups of people are well planned.
sla_teaching_aids: A chart showing points to consider when planning meals for different groups of people
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Different people have different nutritional needs. Students apply nutrition principles to plan meals for groups of people.
sla_notes_details: Principles: include all food groups, suit energy needs, consider age and physiological state, respect budget and availability. Group needs: infants need breast milk and then soft, nutrient-rich complementary foods; school children need energy, protein and calcium; adolescents need extra iron, calcium and energy; pregnant women need folic acid, iron, protein; lactating mothers need extra fluids and energy; adults depend on activity; the elderly need less energy but enough protein, calcium and fibre; the sick need easily digested foods. A plan is written as a menu with three meals and snacks and includes portion sizes and estimated cost.
sla_notes_illustrations: A day menu for an adolescent girl: breakfast of porridge with milk and banana; lunch of rice, beans with spinach; supper of ugali, fish and vegetables; snacks of fruit and groundnuts, giving iron and calcium.
sla_notes_daily_life: Planning meals for household members saves money and matches food to health needs.
sla_exercise: Which mineral is important for pregnant women?::Iron (also folic acid).||Why do adolescents need more energy?::Because of rapid growth and activity.||Name one item in a menu plan.::Meal name, portion size or cost.

sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Cereal dishes are prepared by boiling, steaming, frying and baking. Students describe methods for common dishes.
sla_notes_details: Boiling: rice is washed and boiled in a measured amount of water until tender; ugali is made by stirring flour into boiling water until thick. Steaming: for buns (vitumbua may be fried). Frying: pancakes, chapati, mandazi. Baking: bread, buns. Porridge: flour mixed with cold water, poured into boiling water and stirred. Pilau: rice cooked with meat, onions and spices. Standards: correct measure of water, avoid lumps by stirring, cook until tender not mushy, season well and serve hot. Wash rice only lightly to keep nutrients, use appropriate heat and avoid over-stirring.
sla_notes_illustrations: To cook rice by absorption: for 1 cup of rice, add 2 cups of water, bring to boil, reduce heat, cover and simmer for 15 minutes until water is absorbed.
sla_notes_daily_life: These methods help you prepare staple foods well for the family, for business and for events.
sla_exercise: How much water is used for 1 cup of rice in the absorption method?::About 2 cups.||How do you avoid lumps in porridge?::Mix flour with cold water first and stir while cooking.||Give one dish made by frying cereal dough.::Chapati or mandazi.

sla_notes_intro: Students prepare cereal dishes practically using suitable methods and hygiene.
sla_notes_details: Recipe for chapati: mix 500 g flour, salt and a little oil; add warm water to form dough, knead until soft, rest 20 minutes, divide into balls, roll thin, brush with oil, fold and roll again, cook on a hot pan turning until golden. Recipe for pilau: fry onions, add spices and meat, add washed rice and stock, cook covered on low heat. Recipe for mandazi: mix flour, sugar, yeast or baking powder, coconut milk and cardamom, knead, rest, cut and deep-fry. Assessment: appearance, texture, taste, hygiene, timing and teamwork.
sla_notes_illustrations: Groups prepare pilau, chapati and porridge and present them with a costing sheet showing price per portion.
sla_notes_daily_life: Skills in cereal cookery can be used in small businesses such as selling chapati, mandazi and cooked rice.
sla_exercise: Why rest chapati dough?::To relax the gluten so it can be rolled thinly.||Name two ingredients of pilau.::Rice and spices (meat, onions).||How is a cooked chapati assessed?::By colour, softness, layers and taste.

sla_assessment_criteria: Eggs, fish, meat, milk and milk products are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Food items|Pictures/charts of different food items
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Foods of animal origin are rich in high quality protein. Students study their structure, nutritive value, selection and storage.
sla_notes_details: Eggs: structure is shell, membranes, white (albumen) and yolk; they provide protein, fat, vitamins A, D, B12 and iron; test freshness in water (fresh eggs sink). Fish: white (tilapia), oily (sardines, mackerel) and shellfish; give protein, omega-3 fats and iodine; fresh fish has bright eyes, red gills, firm flesh and no bad smell. Meat: beef, goat, pork, poultry; muscle fibres and connective tissue; gives protein, iron and B vitamins; tender cuts suit grilling and tough cuts stewing. Milk: whole, skimmed, powder, evaporated; provides protein, calcium, vitamin B2 and A. Milk products: yoghurt, cheese, butter, ghee, cream. Store perishables at low temperature and cook thoroughly.
sla_notes_illustrations: To test an egg: place it in water. A fresh egg lies flat at the bottom, a stale one stands upright or floats because of the larger air cell.
sla_notes_daily_life: Choosing and storing animal foods well prevents food poisoning and gives families the protein they need for growth.
sla_exercise: Name the parts of an egg.::Shell, membranes, white and yolk.||Give two milk products.::Yoghurt and cheese (butter, ghee).||How do you recognise fresh fish?::Bright eyes, red gills, firm flesh and fresh smell.

sla_name: Raising agents and their application in cookery
sla_assessment_criteria: Different raising agents and their application in cookery are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Raising agents|Pictures of raising agents
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Raising agents make doughs and batters rise, giving a light texture. Students study types and how they work.
sla_notes_details: Types: biological (yeast, which ferments sugar to produce carbon dioxide), chemical (baking powder, bicarbonate of soda, which release carbon dioxide when moist and heated), and mechanical (air introduced by beating, creaming, whisking, sieving, folding or rolling, and steam). Yeast needs warmth, moisture and food (sugar); it is killed above about 55 degrees Celsius. Baking powder contains bicarbonate and an acid. Uses: yeast in bread and buns; baking powder in cakes and scones; steam in pastry and choux; whisked eggs in sponge cakes. Correct amounts are essential: too much gives a coarse texture or bitter taste.
sla_notes_illustrations: Yeast dough placed in a warm place doubles in size in one hour because carbon dioxide gas is trapped by the gluten network.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding raising agents helps you bake soft bread and cakes and solve problems when baking fails.
sla_exercise: What gas do raising agents produce?::Carbon dioxide.||Give one mechanical raising agent method.::Beating or whisking eggs (sieving flour, creaming).||Why is yeast dough kept warm?::Yeast works best in warmth, so the dough rises faster.

sla_name: Effects of dietary habits on nutritional status
sla_assessment_criteria: Effects of dietary habits on the nutritional status of different groups of people in the society are well explored.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures/videos of malnourished people
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Dietary habits are the regular ways people choose and eat food; they influence nutritional status. Students examine cases in the community.
sla_notes_details: Habits include meal frequency, skipping breakfast, snacking, eating fast food, preference for sweet or salty foods, taboos, and food sharing customs. Good habits (varied diet, regular meals, enough water, fruits and vegetables) lead to good nutritional status; poor habits lead to under- or overnutrition. Groups affected: children (stunting from poor complementary feeding), adolescents (irregular meals, junk food), pregnant women (food taboos reduce protein intake), workers (fast food, obesity), and the elderly (poor appetite). Influences: culture, religion, income, education, media, and availability. Improving habits requires nutrition education, gardens and community action.
sla_notes_illustrations: In a village where children are denied eggs by a food taboo, stunting is common; nutrition education showing the value of eggs can improve children's growth.
sla_notes_daily_life: Changing harmful habits improves health for the whole family and community.
sla_exercise: Give one poor dietary habit.::Skipping breakfast (eating junk food).||How can food taboos affect a pregnant woman?::They can reduce her protein and nutrient intake.||Name a factor that influences food habits.::Culture, income or religion.

sla_assessment_criteria: Different methods of preparing eggs, fish, meat, milk and milk products, vegetables and fruits dishes are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Video showing methods of preparing eggs|Fish|Meat|Milk|Milk products|Vegetables|Fruits dishes
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Different cooking methods suit different foods and preserve nutrients differently. Students describe the methods.
sla_notes_details: Methods: boiling (eggs, meat in stock), simmering and stewing (tough meat, fish stew), steaming (fish, vegetables), frying shallow and deep (eggs, fish, chips), grilling and roasting (meat, fish, corn), baking (fish, custards), poaching (eggs, fish), and sautéing (vegetables). Eggs: boiled for 10 minutes hard, fried, scrambled, poached, omelette. Fish: cleaned, scaled, gutted, marinated in lemon and cooked lightly. Meat: tenderised, marinated, cooked until done. Milk: boiled, used in custards, sauces and yoghurt. Vegetables and fruits: cook briefly to keep colour and vitamins, or serve raw in salads and fruit salad.
sla_notes_illustrations: For a fish stew: clean fish, fry onions and tomatoes, add spices and coconut milk, add fish and simmer 10 minutes until cooked.
sla_notes_daily_life: Choosing the correct method gives tasty, safe and nutritious meals and reduces fuel use.
sla_exercise: Which method is suitable for tough meat?::Stewing (slow, moist cooking).||State a way of cooking eggs.::Boiling, frying or poaching.||Why cook vegetables briefly?::To retain colour and vitamins.

sla_notes_intro: Students practise preparing dishes from these foods with correct techniques and hygiene.
sla_notes_details: Sample dishes: Spanish omelette (eggs, onion, tomato, pepper), fried fish with lemon, beef stew with vegetables, milk pudding or custard, vegetable stir fry, and fruit salad. Procedures include preparing and measuring ingredients, cooking at the right temperature, checking doneness (meat and fish are cooked when juices run clear, fish flakes), seasoning and garnishing. Safety: cook chicken thoroughly, keep milk cool until use, and wash all fruits and vegetables. Evaluate presentation, taste, texture, cost and timekeeping.
sla_notes_illustrations: Students prepare an omelette: beat 2 eggs with salt, fry chopped onion and tomato in a little oil, pour in the eggs, cook until set, fold and serve with a salad.

sla_assessment_criteria: Different methods of preparing bread, cakes, biscuits and buns are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Video showing methods of preparing bread|Cakes|Biscuits|Buns
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Baked products are made using standard methods. Students describe how bread, cakes, biscuits and buns are prepared.
sla_notes_details: Bread: straight dough method, mix flour, yeast, sugar, salt, fat and water; knead, prove, shape, prove again and bake at 220 degrees Celsius. Cakes: creaming method (cream fat and sugar, add eggs, fold in flour), rubbing-in method (rub fat into flour), whisking method (sponge) and all-in-one. Biscuits: rubbing in or creaming, roll, cut and bake at moderate heat. Buns: sweet yeast dough enriched with sugar and fat, shaped and glazed. General rules: preheat the oven, weigh ingredients accurately, grease tins, avoid opening the oven door early, cool on a wire rack.
sla_notes_illustrations: Creaming method for a butter cake: cream 100 g margarine with 100 g sugar until pale, beat in 2 eggs, fold in 200 g self-raising flour, bake at 180 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes.
sla_notes_daily_life: Baking skills are used in home cooking, celebrations and bakery businesses.
sla_exercise: Name two cake-making methods.::Creaming and rubbing-in (whisking).||Why is the oven preheated?::So baking begins at the right temperature and the product rises properly.||What is proving?::Letting shaped dough rise before baking.

sla_assessment_criteria: Raising agents are correctly used in preparing different types of dishes.
sla_teaching_aids: Ingredients|Kitchen equipment|Recipe book/cards
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students bake products with the appropriate raising agents and analyse results.
sla_notes_details: Bread and buns use yeast: activate yeast in warm water with sugar, mix a soft dough, knead 10 minutes, prove until doubled, shape and bake until golden and hollow-sounding. Cakes use baking powder (about 1 teaspoon per 100 g flour) or whisked eggs. Biscuits use baking powder or bicarbonate. Faults: a heavy cake (too little raising agent or over-mixing), a sunken cake (oven opened early, too much raising agent), a dense loaf (dead yeast or insufficient proving). Evaluation covers volume, crumb, crust, taste and appearance.
sla_notes_illustrations: A group bakes yeast buns and baking powder scones; they compare texture, height and taste, and record why the buns are chewier.
sla_notes_daily_life: Using raising agents correctly improves the quality of baked goods that people sell or eat at home.
sla_exercise: Raising agent used in bread?::Yeast.||Give one reason for a sunken cake.::Opening the oven door too early (too much baking powder).||What does a hollow sound when tapping the loaf show?::It is fully baked.

sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: People at different stages of life need different diets. Students prepare meals for children, expectant and lactating mothers, adolescents, invalids, convalescents, vegetarians and the elderly.
sla_notes_details: Children: small frequent meals, energy and protein rich, soft mashed foods for toddlers. Expectant mothers: iron, folic acid, calcium, protein, avoid raw meat and alcohol. Lactating mothers: extra energy and fluids, milk, fruits, vegetables. Adolescents: high energy, iron, calcium. Invalids and convalescents: light, easily digested, attractive, small helpings, high protein for recovery (soups, porridge, custard). Vegetarians: combine pulses, grains, nuts and dairy for complete protein and check B12 and iron. The elderly: soft, less salt and fat, enough fibre and calcium. Plan, cost and prepare meals accordingly.
sla_notes_illustrations: For a convalescent: chicken broth, mashed potatoes with butter, steamed vegetables and baked custard, served in small attractive portions.
sla_notes_daily_life: Preparing suitable meals helps care for family members who are young, old, pregnant or ill.
sla_exercise: Why do pregnant women need folic acid?::It helps the baby's development and prevents neural tube defects.||Give one meal for a convalescent.::Chicken broth or milk pudding (soft, easily digested).||How can vegetarians get complete protein?::By combining pulses, cereals, nuts and dairy foods.

sla_notes_intro: A project is a planned practical activity that applies knowledge and skills. Students design and begin a food and nutrition project.
sla_notes_details: Steps: identify a problem or opportunity (e.g. producing snacks for school, a kitchen garden, promoting balanced diets), set objectives, plan activities, resources, budget and timetable, assign roles, implement, record data, monitor progress and prepare a report. Possible topics: baking and selling healthy snacks, making fruit juice, establishing a school vegetable garden, nutrition education for the community, preserving fruits. Project records include costs, income, quantities, photographs and reflections. Projects are assessed on planning, teamwork, quality of work, creativity and use of resources.
sla_notes_illustrations: A group plans a school snack stall selling fruit salad and groundnuts. They compute costs (fruit 15 000 shillings), set the price, sell for two weeks and record profit.
sla_notes_daily_life: Projects build entrepreneurial skills that help students start income generating activities.
sla_exercise: Name the first step in a project.::Identify the problem or opportunity.||Give two things recorded in a project.::Costs and income (quantities, photographs).||Suggest a food project idea.::Baking and selling healthy snacks or a school vegetable garden.

sla_notes_intro: A packed meal is food prepared to be carried and eaten away from home. Students learn how to plan, pack and choose materials.
sla_notes_details: Packed meals are used for school, work, picnics, journeys, sports and camping. Factors to consider: number of people, occasion and duration, nutritional balance, food that stays safe and attractive without refrigeration, ease of eating, cost, weather, and cultural or dietary restrictions. Suitable foods: sandwiches, boiled eggs, chapati rolls, samosas, cooked drumsticks, fruit, biscuits and juice in bottles. Avoid foods that spoil quickly or leak. Packaging materials: lunch boxes, plastic containers, foil, cling film, wax paper, banana leaves, paper bags and thermos flasks. Materials must be clean, leak-proof, food-grade and, where possible, reusable and environmentally friendly.
sla_notes_illustrations: For a school trip: two chapati rolls with egg filling wrapped in foil, a banana, a small packet of groundnuts and a bottle of water, all packed in a clean lunch box.
sla_notes_daily_life: Well planned packed meals save money compared to buying food outside and keep travellers healthy.

sla_notes_intro: Pastry is a dough of flour, fat and water baked into crisp or flaky products. Students learn its types and uses.
sla_notes_details: Types: shortcrust (rubbing-in method, ratio 2 flour to 1 fat, used for pies and tarts), flaky and rough puff (fat added in pieces and folded, used for sausage rolls), puff (fat layered by folding and rolling, used for cream horns and vol-au-vents), choux (cooked paste with eggs, raised by steam, used for eclairs and profiteroles), suet and hot water crust. Rules for good pastry: keep ingredients and hands cool, handle lightly, use cold water, rest the dough, and bake in a hot oven. Uses: savoury (meat pies, quiches, samosa pastry) and sweet (fruit tarts, pies, turnovers).
sla_notes_illustrations: Shortcrust: rub 100 g margarine into 200 g flour until it looks like breadcrumbs, add cold water to bind, roll out, line a tin and fill with meat or fruit.
sla_notes_daily_life: Pastry making is a valuable skill for bakeries and for preparing snacks for events.
sla_exercise: Name two types of pastry.::Shortcrust and puff pastry (choux, flaky).||Ratio of flour to fat in shortcrust?::2 to 1.||Why keep hands cool when making pastry?::So the fat does not melt, which keeps the pastry light.

sla_notes_intro: Convenience foods are partly or fully prepared foods that save time; leftovers are cooked foods remaining after a meal. Students discuss their use.
sla_notes_details: Convenience foods: canned foods, packaged noodles, frozen vegetables, instant porridge, ready-made sauces, biscuits, ready-mix flours. Advantages: save time and effort, long shelf life, consistent quality and easy storage. Disadvantages: costly, may contain much salt, sugar, fat and additives, less nutritious and produce packaging waste. Leftovers: cool quickly, store covered in a refrigerator, reheat to piping hot, use within one to two days, do not reheat more than once. Reusing leftovers reduces waste and cost, for example leftover rice becomes fried rice and leftover meat becomes samosa filling.
sla_notes_illustrations: Leftover ugali is sliced and fried the next day, and leftover chicken is shredded into a sandwich filling.
sla_notes_daily_life: Using leftovers wisely saves money and reduces food waste in the home and in catering.
sla_exercise: Give two examples of convenience foods.::Canned foods and instant noodles.||State one disadvantage of convenience foods.::They are more expensive and may have added salt or sugar.||How should leftovers be stored?::Cooled quickly, covered and kept in a refrigerator.

sla_notes_intro: Each pastry type is made with a specific method. Students describe these methods and how to avoid faults.
sla_notes_details: Shortcrust: rub fat into flour, add cold water, mix to a dough, rest and roll. Flaky pastry: roll the dough, dot with fat on two thirds, fold in three, rest, repeat three times. Rough puff: cut fat into cubes, mix with flour and water and fold and roll. Puff: enclose a block of fat in dough and give several turns. Choux: boil water and fat, add flour at once and beat, cool, beat in eggs until glossy, pipe and bake at high temperature then lower. Faults: tough pastry (too much water or handling), soggy bottom (too low temperature), shrinkage (stretched dough).
sla_notes_illustrations: To make sausage rolls: roll out rough puff pastry, place sausage meat, fold, seal with egg wash and bake until golden.
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowing the methods helps you produce consistently good pastries for sale or celebrations.
sla_exercise: How is shortcrust pastry made?::By rubbing fat into flour then binding with cold water.||What raises choux pastry?::Steam.||Give one cause of tough pastry.::Too much water or over-handling.

sla_notes_intro: Catering is the business of providing food and drink services to groups. Students study types, menus and costing.
sla_notes_details: Types: commercial (restaurants, hotels, fast-food outlets, mobile caterers), institutional (schools, hospitals, prisons, workplaces), and outside catering (weddings, conferences, parties). Menu planning: consider the customers, occasion, season, budget, nutritional balance, variety of colour, texture and flavour, equipment, staff skills and time; types of menu include table d'hote (fixed price set menu) and a la carte (priced by item). Economics: costing recipes (cost of ingredients divided by portions), selling price = food cost plus labour, overheads and profit margin; control wastage, buy in bulk, and record sales. Percentage gross profit is (selling price minus cost) divided by selling price times 100.
sla_notes_illustrations: If ingredients for 20 portions cost 40 000 shillings, cost per portion is 2 000 shillings; selling at 3 500 gives a profit of 1 500 per portion.
sla_notes_daily_life: Catering skills open opportunities to start food businesses and to manage school and community functions.
sla_exercise: Name two types of catering.::Commercial and institutional (outside).||What is a table d'hote menu?::A set menu at a fixed price.||Cost per portion if 12 portions cost 30 000?::2 500 shillings.

sla_notes_intro: A time plan (work plan) is a schedule showing what to do and when when preparing a meal. Students learn how to prepare one.
sla_notes_details: Importance: ensures all dishes are ready at the right time, organises work and staff, reduces stress, avoids wastage and keeps food hot. Points to consider: number of dishes, cooking times, equipment available, number of people, order of tasks (longest first), serving time, and cleaning. Parts of a time plan: the menu, date and occasion, list of tasks and times (working backwards from serving time), person responsible, equipment and ingredients, and serving and clearing up. Written in columns for time, activity, method and person.
sla_notes_illustrations: For lunch at 1:00 pm: 10:00 prepare vegetables, 10:30 start meat stew, 11:30 cook rice, 12:15 make salad, 12:45 set the table, 1:00 serve.
sla_notes_daily_life: Using a time plan makes it possible to serve family celebrations and events with all food ready at the same time.
sla_exercise: Why work backwards from serving time?::To ensure all dishes are ready together.||Name two parts of a time plan.::Menu and list of tasks with times.||Which tasks are started first?::Those that take longest to cook.

sla_notes_intro: A banquet is a formal, multi-course meal for many guests. Students prepare one following a time plan.
sla_notes_details: Preparation: write the menu (starter, main course, dessert, beverage), calculate quantities, cost, prepare the time plan, assign roles (cooks, servers, cleaners), lay tables and serve. Service: guests are seated, courses served in order from the left or right, plates cleared, water refilled and drinks offered. Standards: hot food hot and cold food cold, attractive garnish, clean uniform, courteous service, and teamwork. Evaluate timing, food quality, presentation, table setting and hygiene. After the event: clean up, count leftovers and review the costing.

sla_notes_intro: Preservation prolongs the life of food by preventing spoilage. Students learn methods and principles.
sla_notes_details: Spoilage is caused by micro-organisms (bacteria, yeasts, moulds), enzymes and chemical changes; they need moisture, warmth, food and oxygen. Principles: remove moisture, lower temperature, add chemicals such as salt, sugar or vinegar, exclude air and kill organisms by heat. Methods: drying (sun-drying fish, vegetables, cereals), refrigeration and freezing, salting and smoking (fish and meat), sugar preservation (jam, syrup), pickling in vinegar, canning and bottling, and fermentation. Importance: reduces losses, provides food in off-season, saves money and allows transport. Storage: store dry foods in airtight containers in cool places and perishables in refrigerators, and apply first-in first-out.
sla_notes_illustrations: Tomatoes plentiful in the season are cooked into paste and bottled or sun-dried, then used months later when prices are high.
sla_notes_daily_life: Preserving food reduces post-harvest losses and helps households and food businesses.
sla_exercise: Name two causes of food spoilage.::Micro-organisms and enzymes.||Give two preservation methods.::Drying and salting (freezing, pickling).||Why apply first-in first-out?::So older stock is used before it spoils.

sla_notes_intro: Students design and use low-cost technologies such as solar dryers, clay pot coolers and smoking kilns to preserve food.
sla_notes_details: Solar dryer: a wooden or wire-mesh frame with a black surface, covered by a transparent plastic sheet, with ventilation, used for drying fruits, vegetables and fish; trays keep food off the ground and protect from dust and insects. Charcoal cooler (evaporative cooler): a double-wall box with wet charcoal or sand between the walls cools by evaporation. Zeer pot: a smaller clay pot inside a larger one with wet sand between. Smoking kiln for fish. Making jam: boil fruit with sugar until setting point, bottle in sterilised jars. Procedure: wash and prepare food, blanch if necessary, dry or process, cool, package airtight, label and store.
sla_notes_illustrations: Slices of mango are blanched, arranged on trays in a solar dryer for two to three days until leathery, then packed in clean bags.
sla_notes_daily_life: Low-cost preservation technologies help farmers and households save produce and earn income.

sla_notes_intro: Students finish the project begun in Form Three and write a report for assessment.
sla_notes_details: A report has: title page, acknowledgement, abstract or summary, introduction (problem and objectives), methodology (activities, resources, timeline), results (data, costs, income, quality of products, photographs), discussion (successes, challenges, lessons learned), conclusion and recommendations, and references or appendices. Assessment considers planning, execution, records, report quality and creativity.
